claim: Open-source energy manager: sends rooftop-PV surplus to the EV, boiler and heat pump.
data_label: open data: Open-Meteo irradiance, Zurich 2024 | simulated house and devices
stats: saved per year vs dumb charging
limit: Simulated house, EV and devices; feed-in price assumed; no real hardware tested yet.
alt: Dark chart. Top: a summer evening and the next day. Solar production is an amber curve; EV charging power is a red spike at plug-in for dumb charging and a green block around midday for the controller. Bottom: monthly PV self-consumption bars, higher with the controller in every month.
post:
Rooftop solar often goes to the grid at a low price while the EV charges from the grid at night.

I built an open-source home energy manager that routes PV surplus into an EV charger (OCPP 1.6J smart charging), a boiler and a heat pump (SG-Ready style signal), with a 25 A per phase house connection limit. It reads a simulated inverter and meter over Modbus TCP and sets charging limits through real OCPP messages to a simulated charge point.

Simulated over one year (Zurich 2024 irradiance from Open-Meteo, 8 kWp, 10 kWh battery, a household with an EV and a heat pump): PV self-consumption 60 % with dumb charging, 75 % with the controller. Cost saved against dumb charging: CHF 214 per year at the ElCom 2024 Zurich tariff and an assumed 8 Rp feed-in. The dumb baseline crossed 25 A on 40 five-minute steps, the controller on 0. Every EV session still reached its target by departure (100 %).

Not verified: no real hardware, a simulated house and driving pattern, an assumed feed-in price, and the limit holds only if the loop reacts faster than the load steps.

What would you check first before trusting a controller like this on a real house?

Code: https://github.com/VB-Builds/pv-surplus-controller
